blocks.text: The speed of a chemical reaction depends on the amount of activation energy required to initiate it. Activation energy is the energy that works to destabilise existing chemical bonds. Enzymes bring the reactants together in the correct orientation, or stress particular chemical bonds of the reactants. In this way they lower the activation energy required for new bonds to form and speed up the rate of the reaction, so reactions proceed much faster than their normal speed.

blocks.title: Activation energy
blocks.text: The energy needed to destabilise the existing chemical bonds of reactants so that a reaction can begin. An enzyme lowers it; it does not change the reactants or products.

blocks.alt: A graph of energy against the progress of a reaction. Reactants start at a higher level than the products. A tall red curve rises between them for the uncatalysed reaction and a lower green curve for the enzyme-catalysed reaction; dashed arrows mark the two activation energies, the green one much shorter.
blocks.caption: Enzymes lower the activation energy (original diagram after Figure 5.2).
blocks.long_description: The reactants must climb an energy hill, the activation energy, before they become products. Without an enzyme the hill is high (red curve); with an enzyme it is much lower (green curve), so more molecules can cross it and the reaction runs faster. The enzyme changes neither the reactants, the products nor the energy difference between them.

blocks.text: The presence of an enzyme does not affect the nature or properties of the end products. Sucrose (the substrate) will always be hydrolysed into glucose and fructose (the products) whether or not sucrase (the enzyme) is present.

Because of its specificity, an enzyme recognises a specific substrate. The substrate binds with the active site of the enzyme, forming an enzyme-substrate complex (ES complex), and the catalytic site is activated. The atoms of the catalytic site stress and destabilise particular bonds of the substrate, so the activation energy is lowered. This action initiates the reaction and the substrate is transformed into products. The enzyme then detaches itself from the products in an unaltered state.

blocks.title: The mechanism in one line
blocks.text: Enzyme + substrate gives the enzyme-substrate complex, which gives enzyme + products.

In complex metabolic pathways such as respiration, photosynthesis and protein synthesis, many enzymes act in a sequence and regulate the steps of the pathway. The successive enzymes controlling these steps are present together along with their cofactors. The products of one enzyme's catalysis serve as the substrate for the enzyme of the next step and are transformed into the next products. The series goes on until the end products are formed, and these inhibit (through feedback) the first enzyme.
Models for the mechanism of enzyme action

In 1894 the German chemist Emil Fischer proposed the lock-and-key model: as a specific key can open only a specific lock, so a specific enzyme can transform only one specific substrate into products. This model postulates that the active site is a rigid structure, with no modification or flexibility before, during or after the enzyme action.

Later studies did not support the lock-and-key model in all reactions. On the basis of new evidence the American biochemist Daniel Koshland (1958) presented the induced fit model: when a substrate combines with the binding site of an enzyme, it induces changes in the enzyme's structure, and these changes enable the enzyme to perform its catalytic activity more effectively. This model postulates that the active site is not rigid but is capable of modification and flexibility before the enzyme action (catalysis) starts.

blocks.alt: Top row, lock and key: a square substrate drops into a square notch in a rigid enzyme, forms the enzyme-substrate complex, and leaves as two products with the enzyme unchanged. Bottom row, induced fit: a rounded substrate approaches a loosely matching hollow; the enzyme's sides bend in to grip it exactly; the products leave and the site relaxes.
blocks.caption: The lock-and-key model and the induced fit model (original diagram after Figures 5.3 and 5.4).
blocks.long_description: In Fischer's lock-and-key model (1894) the active site is a rigid shape that only its one substrate matches, like a key in a lock; the substrate binds, is converted, and the enzyme is unchanged. In Koshland's induced fit model (1958) the active site is flexible: binding the substrate changes the enzyme's shape so that it grips the substrate and catalyses more effectively, and the site relaxes when the products leave.
